primitives.name: Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium
primitives.verbatim_quote: In this study, genotypic and allelic frequencies were determined in 452 subjects: 292 professional athletes (160 elite endurance athletes and 132 professional football players) and 160 non-athlete subjects.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'p, q': 'allele frequencies in diploid populations', 'p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1': 'equilibrium condition'}
primitives.assumptions: No mutation, migration, selection, or drift; random mating.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When evolutionary forces disrupt equilibrium or sample size is insufficient.

layer2.mapping: HWE provides normalization constraint for estimating allele frequencies in athlete populations.

The core derivation begins with the assumption that athletic performance is influenced by a set of genetic polymorphisms, each contributing additively to an individual's capacity. Genotype scoring (GS) aggregates these contributions into a total genotype score (TGS), which is then compared across groups—professional athletes versus non-athletes. Statistical significance (p<0.001) indicates that the distribution of TGS differs meaningfully between groups, suggesting a genetic basis for athletic talent. The Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium ensures that observed genotype frequencies reflect true population genetics rather than sampling bias. These primitives form a dual framework: one for identifying predictive genetic signatures (polygenic profile), and another for validating the statistical robustness of those signatures (HWE). Failure modes include epistasis, population stratification, or confounding due to environmental variables not captured in the model.
